stem: Which lesion site pattern is most consistent with Ewing sarcoma rather than osteosarcoma in an adolescent?

options.text: Lesion centred at the diaphysis of a long bone or in the pelvis
Lesion at the distal femoral growth end
Lesion at the proximal tibial growth end
Lesion at the proximal humeral growth end
Lesion centred in the rib shaft

explanation: Ewing sarcoma is typically centred in the diaphysis of long bones or the pelvis, whereas osteosarcoma usually arises at the growing ends of long bones.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

rationale: Ewing sarcoma favours diaphyseal and axial locations, while osteosarcoma favours the metaphyseal growing ends of long bones.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because Ewing sarcoma commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones or the pelvis.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because the distal femur is a classic osteosarcoma site at the growing end of a long bone.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the proximal tibia is a common osteosarcoma location near the growth plate.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the proximal humerus is another typical osteosarcoma site at the metaphysis.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because rib involvement can occur with Ewing sarcoma, but the more specific classic pattern is a diaphyseal long-bone or pelvic lesion.
